newsitem.title: USA: Securities group faults SEC's mutual fund reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Securities group faults SEC's mutual fund reform plan.

text.p: Leaders of the securities industry are urging the Securities and Exchange Commission to soften its proposal requiring firms to use "plain English" in the documents they distribute to investors.
The proposal should only be a recommendation and not a requirement, the Securities Industry Association said.

"We cannot support a rule that would mandate plain English usage in prospectuses, as opposed to one that merely would recommend it," the Securities Industry Association wrote in an April 24 letter to the agency.

In February, the SEC unanimously agreed to consider the plan, which includes redesigning often technical and lengthy mutual fund prospectuses, the documents investors receive outlining a fund's strategy and risks.
The proposal -- the culmination of a two-and-a half year-old initiative -- is designed to encourage investors to take a closer and more informed look at the investments they make.

Changes to these documents, which contain essential information about the investments, fees and style of mutual funds, will make them "simpler, clearer, more useful, and we hope, more used," the agency's Chairman Arthur Levitt told the mutual fund industry in Boston last month.
But the Securities Industry Association fears that trimmed down and less technical disclosures may expose firms to lawsuits.

"There are a variety of reasons why many prospectuses are written in a legalistic and dense manner," the association wrote, noting that the documents are meant to also satisfy legal and regulatory requirements.

"Prohibiting the use of all legal jargon and technical business terms in all contexts is inadvisable," the association warned. "Such a prohibition would expose issuers to greater liablity and result in the omission of certain information that some investors may want."

Siegel & Gale, the New York-based marketing and communications firm that says it has pioneered the idea of plain English disclosure, has developed the SEC handbook companies would turn to do comply with the new rules.
The firm's President, Kenneth Morris, faulted SIA's concerns. "I was very disappointed in the SIA's response because it seems to run counter to all their initiatives to educate investors," he said.
"The truth of the matter is while you really can't legislate clarity, if this is not mandated it will not be done on a voluntary basis," Morris added.
